# SPI Host Core Controller Design Specification

## 1. Overview

This block is the core control state machine for the SPI host. It accepts command-segment descriptors from software, generates correctly timed SPI bus activity, and coordinates the flow of data through the attached shift-register datapath.

The block itself does not store or serialize SPI data. It produces control pulses and status indications that tell the surrounding datapath when to load, shift, sample, and unload data.

The block supports:

- Any number of chip-select lines, selected by a chip-select identifier.
- Standard, Dual, and Quad SPI speeds.
- TX-only, RX-only, bidirectional, and dummy segments.
- All SPI clock polarity and phase combinations.
- Full-cycle sampling mode.
- Automatic chip-select timing, including lead, trail, and idle delays.
- Back-to-back segment execution with chip-select hold.
- Safe chip-select and clock configuration switching.
- Stall behavior when the datapath cannot provide or accept data.

## 2. Reset and Enable Behavior

### 2.1 Hardware Reset

After reset, the block must:

- Return to the inactive idle state.
- Deassert all chip-select outputs.
- Stop the serial clock and hold it at its default inactive level.
- Clear all transaction state, including byte, bit, and delay counters.
- Deassert all data-path control pulses.
- Deassert the active status indicator.
- Not accept commands.

### 2.2 Enable Input

The block must not begin operation until the enable input is asserted.

When the enable input is deasserted:

- The block must not accept new commands.
- The block must not generate serial clock pulses.
- The block must not change the state of any chip-select output.
- The block must not issue data-path control pulses.
- If the block is in the middle of a transaction, it must freeze in its current state and resume when the enable input is asserted again.

### 2.3 Software Reset

A software reset request must take priority over all other operation.

While software reset is asserted, the block must:

- Terminate any in-progress transaction immediately.
- Return to the inactive idle state.
- Deassert all chip-select outputs.
- Hold the serial clock at its inactive level.
- Clear all internal counters.
- Deassert all data-path control pulses.
- Remain in this state until software reset is removed.

Software reset must not require the normal trail or idle delay before returning to idle.

## 3. Command Intake

### 3.1 Command Descriptor Contents

Each command segment descriptor contains the following information:

- The target chip-select identifier.
- Clock configuration settings:
  - Clock polarity.
  - Clock phase.
  - Full-cycle sampling enable.
  - Clock divider value.
  - Chip-select lead, trail, and idle timing values.
- Segment length, expressed in bytes.
- Segment direction:
  - TX-only.
  - RX-only.
  - Bidirectional.
  - Dummy.
- Segment speed:
  - Standard.
  - Dual.
  - Quad.
- Chip-select-active-after-transfer (CSAAT) flag.

### 3.2 Command Acceptance

The block must accept a new command only when:

- The block is enabled.
- The command valid input is asserted.
- The command-ready output is asserted.
- The block is not stalled.

The command-ready output must be suppressed during any stall condition, even if the block would otherwise be ready.

The block must be ready to accept a command in the following situations:

- In the inactive idle state.
- In the chip-select-active idle state.
- At the end of a CSAAT segment when the next command is already present and targets the same chip-select line.
- At the end of the idle delay after a normal transaction, if a command is already pending.

A command accepted by the block must be captured and used as the basis for the next segment or transaction.

## 4. Clock Generation

### 4.1 Clock Divider

The serial clock must be generated from the core clock using the clock divider value supplied in the command configuration.

The block advances its state only at divided-clock boundaries. One timing timeslice is equal to:

```text
core clock period × (clock divider value + 1)
```

The serial clock must be high for one timeslice and low for one timeslice while data is being transferred.

While the block is in an idle state, the clock divider must be held at zero so that a newly accepted command can begin immediately without waiting for a divider timeout.

### 4.2 Clock Polarity

The clock polarity setting determines the inactive level of the serial clock.

- If clock polarity is 0:
  - The serial clock idles low.
  - Active data pulses drive the clock high.
- If clock polarity is 1:
  - The serial clock idles high.
  - Active data pulses drive the clock low.

The serial clock must not produce pulses during chip-select lead, trail, idle, or configuration-switch periods.

## 5. Transaction Execution

### 5.1 Normal Transaction, Single Segment

When a command is accepted from the inactive idle state, the block must:

1. Assert the selected chip-select output low.
2. Hold the selected chip-select low for the configured lead time.
3. Begin generating serial clock pulses.
4. Execute the requested segment.
5. At the end of the segment, stop the serial clock.
6. Hold the selected chip-select low for the configured trail time.
7. Deassert all chip-select outputs high.
8. Hold all chip-select outputs high for the configured idle time.
9. Return to the inactive idle state.

The lead, trail, and idle timings must each have a duration of at least the configured value plus one timeslice.

### 5.2 Segment Length and Speed

The segment length is expressed in bytes.

The number of serial clock cycles required for one byte depends on the segment speed:

- Standard speed: 8 clock cycles per byte.
- Dual speed: 4 clock cycles per byte.
- Quad speed: 2 clock cycles per byte.

The block must track the number of bytes remaining in the current segment and the number of bit-groups remaining in the current byte.

When the current byte and the current segment are both complete, the block must end the segment according to the CSAAT flag.

### 5.3 Direction Behavior

The block must behave as follows for each segment direction:

- TX-only:
  - Request a new byte from the transmit datapath at the start of each byte.
  - Do not generate receive-side read requests.

- RX-only:
  - Generate receive-side read requests at the end of each received byte.
  - Do not request transmit bytes.

- Bidirectional:
  - Request a new byte at the start of each byte.
  - Generate a receive-side read request at the end of each byte.

- Dummy:
  - Generate only serial clock cycles.
  - Do not issue transmit byte requests.
  - Do not issue receive-side read requests.

### 5.4 CSAAT and Back-to-Back Segments

When the CSAAT flag is set, the block must hold the selected chip-select output low after the current segment finishes.

If the next command is already present and targets the same chip-select line, the block must start the next segment immediately, with:

- No trail delay.
- No idle delay.
- No lead delay.
- No deassertion of the chip-select output.

The serial clock must continue without an unnecessary pause.

If no next command is present at the end of a CSAAT segment, the block must enter the chip-select-active idle state:

- The selected chip-select output remains low.
- The serial clock stops at its inactive level.
- The active status indicator is deasserted.
- The block is ready to accept another command.

### 5.5 End of Transaction with CSAAT Cleared

When the CSAAT flag is cleared, the current segment marks the end of the transaction.

The block must:

- Stop the serial clock.
- Apply the configured trail delay.
- Deassert all chip-select outputs high.
- Apply the configured idle delay.
- Return to the inactive idle state, or begin a pending next command after the idle delay.

## 6. Chip-Select Behavior

### 6.1 Inactive State

In the inactive idle state, all chip-select outputs must be deasserted high.

### 6.2 Selected Chip-Select

When a transaction starts, only the chip-select output corresponding to the command’s chip-select identifier must be asserted low.

All other chip-select outputs must remain high.

### 6.3 Chip-Select-Active Idle

In the chip-select-active idle state, the selected chip-select output must remain low.

This state is still considered idle for status reporting, even though a chip-select line is asserted.

### 6.4 Switching to a Different Chip-Select

If a new command targets a different chip-select line while the current chip-select is held active, the block must first close out the current transaction.

The block must:

- Stop the serial clock.
- Apply the old device’s trail delay.
- Deassert all chip-select outputs high.
- Apply the old device’s idle delay.
- Only then apply the new device’s configuration and assert the new chip-select output.

The new command must not be acknowledged until the closing trail and idle delays have completed.

## 7. Configuration Switching

### 7.1 When Configuration Switching Is Required

If a command is accepted from the inactive idle state, or after a normal trailing idle period, and its clock configuration differs from the previously latched configuration, the block must insert an additional configuration-switch delay before starting the next segment.

A configuration change includes changes to:

- Clock polarity.
- Clock phase.
- Full-cycle sampling mode.
- Clock divider.
- Chip-select lead, trail, or idle timing values.

### 7.2 Behavior During Configuration Switch

During the configuration-switch delay:

- All chip-select outputs must be high.
- The serial clock must stay at its inactive level.
- No data-path control pulses may be generated.

The configuration-switch delay must be at least the new idle timing value plus one timeslice.

The new configuration must become active only while all chip-select outputs are high.

## 8. Data-Path Control

### 8.1 Byte Write Request

The block must issue a write-request pulse when a new byte must be loaded into the shift register for transmission.

Write requests must be generated for:

- TX-only segments.
- Bidirectional segments.

Write requests must not be generated for:

- RX-only segments.
- Dummy segments.

### 8.2 Shift Pulses

The block must issue shift pulses to advance the shift register by the appropriate number of bits for the current speed:

- Standard speed: shift by 1 bit.
- Dual speed: shift by 2 bits.
- Quad speed: shift by 4 bits.

Shift pulses must be timed so that the next group of bits appears on the data lines at the correct serial clock edge.

### 8.3 Byte Read Request

The block must issue a read-request pulse when a complete byte must be transferred from the shift register to the receive datapath.

Read requests must be generated for:

- RX-only segments.
- Bidirectional segments.

Read requests must not be generated for:

- TX-only segments.
- Dummy segments.

### 8.4 Sample Pulses

The block must issue sample pulses to capture data from the SPI data lines.

Sample pulses must be generated for segments that receive data.

In normal mode, the sample pulse must occur one half serial clock period after the active clock edge.

In full-cycle mode, the sample pulse must occur one full serial clock period after the active clock edge.

### 8.5 Clock Phase Alignment

The block must align write, shift, read, and sample pulses according to the selected clock phase.

- With clock phase 0:
  - The first transmit byte is requested as the chip-select line is asserted.
  - Data shifts and sampling align with the leading edge of the serial clock.
- With clock phase 1:
  - The first transmit byte is requested after the first serial clock edge.
  - Data shifts and sampling align with the trailing edge of the serial clock.

## 9. Data-Line Output Enables

The data-line output enables control which SPI data lines are driven by the host.

### 9.1 No Chip-Select Active

When no chip-select output is asserted, all data-line output enables must be deasserted.

### 9.2 Standard Speed

In Standard speed, the first data line must be enabled as an output whenever a chip-select output is active.

This is true regardless of whether the segment is TX-only, RX-only, bidirectional, or dummy.

### 9.3 Dual Speed

In Dual speed:

- If the segment is transmit-capable, the first two data-line output enables must be asserted.
- If the segment is not transmit-capable, no data-line output enables may be asserted.

### 9.4 Quad Speed

In Quad speed:

- If the segment is transmit-capable, all four data-line output enables must be asserted.
- If the segment is not transmit-capable, no data-line output enables may be asserted.

## 10. Stall Behavior

### 10.1 Transmit Stall

The block must assert a transmit-stall condition when it needs to write a new byte to the shift register but the transmit datapath is not ready to provide the byte.

### 10.2 Receive Stall

The block must assert a receive-stall condition when it has a completed received byte to transfer to the receive datapath but the receive datapath is not ready to accept the byte.

### 10.3 Effect of Stall

When either stall condition is active, the block must:

- Freeze all state transitions.
- Freeze all byte, bit, and delay counters.
- Hold the serial clock at its current level.
- Hold all chip-select outputs at their current level.
- Suppress all data-path control pulses.
- Suppress command-ready indication.

When the stall condition clears, the block must resume operation from the point where it stopped.

## 11. Status and Indication Outputs

### 11.1 Active Status

The active status output must indicate whether the block is processing a transaction.

The active status must be asserted when the block is in any non-idle state, including:

- Lead delay.
- Active clock generation.
- Trail delay.
- Idle delay.
- Configuration-switch delay.

The active status must be deasserted when the block is in:

- The inactive idle state.
- The chip-select-active idle state.

### 11.2 Speed Indication

The block must output the speed of the current segment so that the datapath can select the correct shift width and data-line mapping.

### 11.3 Full-Cycle Indication

The block must output the full-cycle mode flag of the current configuration so that the datapath can use the correct sample timing.

### 11.4 Last-Read Indication

The block must assert the last-read indication when the final byte of a receive-capable segment is being transferred to the receive datapath.

The last-read indication must only be asserted when the receive datapath is ready to accept the byte.

### 11.5 Last-Write Indication

The block must assert the last-write indication when the final byte of a transmit-capable segment is being loaded from the transmit datapath.

The last-write indication must only be asserted when the transmit datapath is ready to provide the byte.

## 12. Assumptions and Constraints

The block assumes that command descriptors are valid.

In particular:

- The chip-select identifier must be in range.
- The speed must be Standard, Dual, or Quad; the reserved speed value must not be used.
- Bidirectional segments are valid only in Standard speed.

The block does not generate error responses for invalid descriptors.
